concepts.name: Training data
concepts.explanation: The examples a model learns from. Its quality, size and how well it represents real use matter as much as the algorithm.
concepts.caveat: More data does not fix biased or mislabelled data; it can reinforce the same errors at scale.
concepts.question: Why could a model trained on a million examples still fail for a group of users?

concepts.name: Features
concepts.explanation: The measurable inputs a model uses, such as pixel values, word tokens or a customer's purchase count.
concepts.caveat: Deep learning learns many features itself, but choosing what data to include is still a human decision with effects.
concepts.question: What feature could secretly stand in for a protected attribute like race?

concepts.name: Supervised learning
concepts.explanation: Learning from examples paired with correct answers (labels), to predict the label for new inputs.
concepts.caveat: Labels are created by people and processes, so they carry their mistakes and assumptions.
concepts.question: Who decided what the "correct" label was in your dataset, and could they be wrong?

concepts.name: Unsupervised learning
concepts.explanation: Finding structure in data without labels, such as grouping similar items (clustering) or compressing data.
concepts.caveat: Clusters found by an algorithm are not automatically meaningful categories in the real world.
concepts.question: How would you check whether a discovered cluster means anything?

concepts.name: Model
concepts.explanation: A function with adjustable parameters that maps inputs to outputs; training sets the parameters so outputs match the data.
concepts.caveat: A model learns patterns in its data, not causes; correlation it picks up may not hold when conditions change.
concepts.question: Why might a model that predicts well fail when you use it to decide on an intervention?

concepts.name: Loss function
concepts.explanation: A number that measures how wrong the model's predictions are; training tries to make it as small as possible.
concepts.caveat: The loss is a proxy for what you care about; optimising it hard can produce behaviour you did not intend.
concepts.question: What could go wrong if a model is trained only to maximise clicks?

concepts.name: Gradient descent
concepts.explanation: An optimisation method that repeatedly nudges parameters in the direction that most reduces the loss.
concepts.caveat: It finds a good enough solution, not necessarily the best; in large networks that usually turns out to be fine.
concepts.question: What happens if the step size (learning rate) is far too large?

concepts.name: Neural network
concepts.explanation: A model made of layers of simple units with weighted connections, able to represent very complex functions.
concepts.caveat: Despite the name, they are loosely inspired by brains, not models of how brains work.
concepts.question: Why might a deeper network learn features that a shallow one cannot?

concepts.name: Backpropagation
concepts.explanation: The algorithm that efficiently computes how each weight in a neural network affects the loss, so gradient descent can update them.
concepts.caveat: Backpropagation computes gradients; it is not itself the learning rule or the optimiser.
concepts.question: Why was efficient gradient computation essential for training networks with millions of weights?

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.explanation: When a model learns noise and quirks of the training data, scoring well there but poorly on new data.
concepts.caveat: Very large modern models can fit training data perfectly and still generalise, which complicates the classic picture.
concepts.question: What is the clearest sign that a model is overfitting?

concepts.name: Generalisation
concepts.explanation: How well a model performs on new data it has not seen, which is the real goal of learning.
concepts.caveat: Good test scores only show generalisation to data like the test set, not to every real-world situation.
concepts.question: Why might a model ace its test set and still fail in deployment?

concepts.name: Bias-variance tradeoff
concepts.explanation: Simple models may miss real patterns (bias); flexible models may chase noise (variance). Good models balance the two.
concepts.caveat: In deep learning the simple U-shaped picture does not always hold.
concepts.question: Which would you expect to have higher variance: a straight line or a 20th-degree polynomial?

concepts.name: Regularization
concepts.explanation: Techniques that discourage over-complex models, such as penalising large weights, dropout or stopping training early.
concepts.caveat: Regularization reduces overfitting but too much of it causes the model to miss real patterns.
concepts.question: Why might stopping training early act like a regularizer?

concepts.name: Train-test split
concepts.explanation: Holding back some data the model never trains on, so performance can be measured honestly on unseen examples.
concepts.caveat: Tuning repeatedly against the test set slowly leaks it into training; a separate validation set helps.
concepts.question: Why should you not choose your final model by checking the test set over and over?

concepts.name: Data leakage
concepts.explanation: When information that would not be available at prediction time sneaks into training, making results look far better than reality.
concepts.caveat: Leakage is easy to miss: duplicate records, future data or features computed from the label can all cause it.
concepts.question: A model predicting hospital outcomes scores 99%. What leakage would you look for first?

concepts.name: Hyperparameters
concepts.explanation: Settings chosen before training, such as learning rate, model size or regularization strength, rather than learned from data.
concepts.caveat: Extensive tuning can overfit to the validation set, giving optimistic results.
concepts.question: How is a hyperparameter different from a model weight?
